960.title: Repel with better
960.hook: repel evil with what is better, and your enemy may become a close friend (Quran 41:34)
960.carry: a door opening where a wall stood
960.howItsDone: Muslims recite and memorize Qur'an 41:34–35, and teachers and preachers quote it when urging people to answer insult or hostility with good conduct.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mistah, and a verse that asked: wouldn't you love to be forgiven? Did one withdrawn kindness go back out? Today, the last of these Muslim voices, and a verse about how to answer harm. Day nine hundred sixty.

Two sentences sit side by side in the Qur'an, in chapter forty-one. The first sounds obvious: the good deed and the bad deed are not alike. The second is an instruction with a surprise inside it. In paraphrase: push back the bad with what is better, and the one with whom you had hostility will be as though a close, warm friend. Not endure it. Not walk away from it. Push it back. The verb has force. What it pushes with is the unexpected part. Today: repel with better.
screen: `GOOD AND BAD ARE NOT ALIKE.` → `PUSH BACK THE BAD.` → `WITH WHAT IS BETTER.`

segments.voice: First, the push. The Arabic command is idfa', push back, ward off. The verse isn't asking anyone to lie down and be walked on. Harm is to be met and turned back. Second, the tool. What does the pushing is, in the verse's words in paraphrase, that which is better. Not equal. Not the same coin handed back. Better. A harsh word met with a calm one. A slight met with a fairness the other person didn't expect. Third, the result. In the verse's picture, the enemy becomes as though a close friend. As though: the verse chooses its words with care. A door opening where a wall stood. Fourth, the cost. The very next verse, forty-one thirty-five, says this is granted only to those who are patient, and to those who have a great share of good. So the Qur'an itself admits this is hard. It isn't presented as a trick that always works. It's described as something given to the patient. Some Muslim commentators read this verse alongside others that allow a just response to a wrong, and teach repelling with better as the higher road within that. So this verse is less a rule for easy days than one for the next sharp word, whenever it comes. Tomorrow the theme turns to Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist and Chinese voices.
screen: `PUSH THE HARM BACK.` · `WITH WHAT IS BETTER.` · `AN ENEMY, LIKE A CLOSE FRIEND.` · `ONLY THE PATIENT.` · then, large: `REPEL WITH BETTER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring back one harsh thing said to you recently. A comment at work. A message in a group chat. A tone at the dinner table. Hear it once, then let it go quiet. Now, instead of the answer you gave or wished you'd given, look for something better. Not weaker. Better. A calm sentence. A question. A fairness they didn't expect. Hold that answer, and notice how it sits. If you pray, you can ask for patience in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Idfa'. Push back, ward off: the Arabic command behind repelling harm with what is better, until the enemy becomes as though a friend. Today's word.
Your line: a door opening where a wall stood. The next time something sharp comes at you today, push it back with something better than what came. Day nine hundred sixty.

961.title: Kshama, forbearance
961.hook: the Gita lists forgiveness among the divine qualities (Bhagavad Gita 16.3)
961.howItsDone: Hindus read the Bhagavad Gita's list of divine qualities in chapter 16 as a picture of the character to grow toward, and kshama, forgiveness or forbearance, is taught as one of them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, idfa': push harm back with something better than what came. What did you answer with? Today the theme turns to Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist and Chinese voices, starting with one Sanskrit word. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

Kshama. The word turns up in a list, which is an odd place to meet something so hard to do. In the sixteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna about two kinds of nature a person can be born to, one he calls divine and one demonic, and he names the divine qualities first, one after another, like things packed for a long journey. Fearlessness. Purity of heart. Generosity. Self-control. Truthfulness. Freedom from anger. And near the end of the list, in the third verse, kshama. Today: kshama, forbearance.
screen: `A WORD IN A LIST.` → `THE DIVINE QUALITIES.` → `NEAR THE END: KSHAMA.`

segments.voice: First, the neighbors. Kshama doesn't stand alone. In the same verse, right beside it, are vigor and fortitude, the strength to keep going under pressure. A little earlier comes freedom from anger. Forgiveness here keeps strong company. It isn't listed among the soft extras; it's packed in with the steel. Second, the meaning. Kshama is translated as forgiveness, and also as forbearance or patience: the capacity to bear what's done to you without striking back. Less a single act after a fight, more a settled way of holding wrongs as they come. Third, the setting. Krishna says this on a battlefield, to a man about to go to war. So the Gita isn't describing someone with no enemies, sitting somewhere peaceful. It's describing a person who may have to act, even firmly, and still carries forbearance inside. Hindu teachers read that tension in different ways, and the Gita leaves room for them. Fourth, whose quality it is. Kshama is listed as a mark of the one who forgives. Nothing in the verse makes it wait on the other person's apology, or on their deserving it. It's described as part of a divine nature, and some teachers read the list as something a person can grow into. That turns the usual question around. Not, have they earned my forgiveness? But, what kind of nature am I growing?
screen: `STRONG NEIGHBORS IN THE LIST.` · `FORGIVENESS AND FORBEARANCE.` · `SPOKEN ON A BATTLEFIELD.` · `A MARK OF THE ONE WHO FORGIVES.` · then, large: `KSHAMA.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Think ahead through the rest of today. Somewhere in it, someone is likely to irritate you: a driver, a coworker, a family member, a slow line. Picture that moment arriving. Feel the small heat that comes with it. Now picture yourself bearing it. Not pretending it's fine. Just letting it arrive, and pass through, without striking back. Breathe out slowly, as if making room. If you pray, you can ask for kshama in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Kshama. Sanskrit for forgiveness and forbearance, listed among the divine qualities in the Bhagavad Gita, beside vigor and fortitude. Today's word.
Your line: packed in with the steel. When the irritation comes today, forbear once: let it pass without striking back, and notice the strength it takes. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

962.title: Where forgiveness is
962.hook: Kabir, in the Guru Granth Sahib: where there is forgiveness, there is God (Guru Granth Sahib 1372)
962.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing Kabir's saloks as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and this couplet on forgiveness (Ang 1372) is quoted in Sikh teaching on khima.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kshama: forbearance, listed among the divine qualities in the Gita, beside vigor and fortitude. Where did you forbear once? Today, the same idea in the Sikh scripture, from a weaver poet. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

Turn toward the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, to page thirteen seventy-two. There's a run of short couplets there, saloks, by Kabir, the weaver poet whose verses the Sikh Gurus gathered into their book. One of them is built like a map. Where this is, there's that. Where this other thing is, there's that other thing. Pair after pair, plain as directions to a neighbor's house. Then the last pair changes what kind of map it is. Today: where forgiveness is.

First, the map. In paraphrase, Kabir says: where there is spiritual wisdom, there is righteousness. Where there is falsehood, there is sin. Where there is greed, there is death. And where there is forgiveness, there is God himself. Second, the shape. The first pairs read like cause and effect. Wisdom leads to right living. Lies lead to wrongdoing. Greed leads to ruin. Then the last pair breaks the pattern. Forgiveness doesn't lead to a reward, or a better mood, or a good reputation. It's the place where God is found. Third, the two words. The word for forgiveness in the Gurmukhi text is khima. And the word at the very end, for God, is aap: himself, God's own self. Not a gift sent from God to the forgiving person. God, present, where forgiveness is happening. Fourth, the home. This couplet is by Kabir, not one of the Sikh Gurus. Yet it sits in the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs honor as their living Guru, alongside the Gurus' own hymns. The Gurus included voices from beyond their own circle, Hindu and Muslim saints among them, where those voices said what the Gurus heard as true. So a weaver's line about forgiveness is sung and read in gurdwaras as scripture. Put the couplet next to yesterday's. The Gita listed kshama as a quality of divine nature. Kabir puts it as a place: find forgiveness, and you've found where God is.
screen: `WHERE THIS IS, THERE IS THAT.` · `THE LAST PAIR BREAKS THE PATTERN.` · `KHIMA, AND AAP.` · `A WEAVER'S VOICE IN THE GURU.` · then, large: `WHERE FORGIVENESS IS, GOD HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Find one small thing to forgive, right now, something from this week. A late reply. A borrowed thing returned scratched. A remark at dinner. Bring it up clearly. Then let it go, here, in this sitting, the way you'd set a cup down. Don't wait to feel finished. Just set it down. Then stay with the space where it was for a few breaths. If you pray, you can say a line of Kabir's or your own tradition's words. If not, simply rest there. The bell holds the time.
Khima. Kabir's word for forgiveness in the Guru Granth Sahib, from the couplet where there is forgiveness, there is God himself. Today's word.
Your line: God's own self, present there. Forgive one small thing today on the spot, without waiting, and take a breath where it was. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiveness is a nice thing to do.

963.title: Angulimala stops
963.hook: a murderer wearing a necklace of fingers meets the Buddha, stops, and becomes a monk (Majjhima Nikaya 86)
963.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the story of Angulimala from the Majjhima Nikaya as a sign that even a killer can change, and some Buddhists chant verses from the same sutta, linked to Angulimala and a woman in labor, as a blessing for childbirth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's word khima: where forgiveness is, there is God himself. What small thing did you set down? Today, a far bigger wrong, from the Buddhist texts, and a man a whole countryside feared. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

A road through a forest in the kingdom of Kosala, and the people along it are afraid. The sutta says villages and towns have been laid waste. A killer lives in those trees, and he wears a garland made of his victims' fingers. People call him Angulimala. One morning a monk walks down that road alone. Cowherds and farmers shout at him to turn around. He keeps walking, in silence. The monk is the Buddha. Today: Angulimala stops.
screen: `AN EMPTY ROAD.` → `A GARLAND OF FINGERS.` → `A MONK WALKS IN ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the chase. Angulimala sees the monk coming, takes up his sword and shield, and runs after him. Then something strange happens, in the sutta's telling: he runs as hard as he can, and can't catch up with the Buddha, who is only walking at his usual pace. Out of breath, he shouts: stop, monk! Second, the answer. The Buddha keeps walking and says, in paraphrase: I have stopped, Angulimala. You stop too. Angulimala is baffled. The monk is plainly still walking. So the Buddha explains: he has stopped harming living beings, for good. Angulimala hasn't. Third, the turn. Angulimala throws his weapons away into a chasm, bows at the Buddha's feet, and asks to become a monk. The Buddha says, come, monk, and that's his ordination. Later King Pasenadi rides out with soldiers to hunt the killer, and finds him sitting quietly in robes among the monks. The king is astonished. Fourth, the cost. The sutta doesn't pretend it's easy. Walking for alms one day, Angulimala is hit by thrown stones and comes back bleeding, his bowl broken. The Buddha tells him to bear it: this is the fruit of what he did, ripening now. So the change is real, and the past is real too. The sutta holds both. In a week about forgiveness, this is a case with blood on it, and the Buddha's first words to him were neither an excuse nor a sentence. They were: you stop too.
screen: `HE CAN'T CATCH A WALKING MONK.` · `I HAVE STOPPED. YOU STOP TOO.` · `A KILLER IN ROBES.` · `STONES ON THE ALMS ROUND.` · then, large: `HE STOPPED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Think of one person you've quietly written off. Someone you've decided is just like that and always will be. It doesn't have to be dramatic. A relative. An old friend. A public figure. Hold their face for a moment. Then, without excusing anything they did, try one sentence in your mind: this person could stop. Notice what that does to the picture you carry of them. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Angulimala stops. The killer who couldn't catch a walking monk, heard I have stopped, you stop too, and threw his weapons away. Today's word.
Your line: he stopped. Today, when someone you've written off comes to mind, give them one moment of believing they could change. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

964.title: The unaccepted gift
964.hook: abused by a visitor, the Buddha asks: if a gift isn't accepted, whose is it? (Samyutta Nikaya 7.2)
964.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers retell this sutta, known as the Akkosa Sutta, when teaching patience: insults are heard but not accepted, and not returned.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Angulimala stopped: a killer threw his weapons away and became a monk. Your line was he stopped. Did you let one person be more than their worst? Today, the Buddha, and an insult thrown to his face. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

If you bring someone a gift and they don't take it, who owns it? It sounds like a riddle for children. In the Samyutta Nikaya, it's the heart of the Buddha's reply to a man who has just stood in front of him and cursed him. The man is a brahmin of the Bharadvaja clan. He's heard that someone from his clan has left home to become a monk under the Buddha, and he is furious. So he goes to find the Buddha and abuses him to his face, with rude and harsh words. Today: the unaccepted gift.
screen: `A RIDDLE ABOUT A GIFT.` → `A FURIOUS VISITOR.` → `ABUSE, TO HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: First, the question. The Buddha doesn't answer the insults, and he doesn't go silent either. He asks: do friends and relatives ever come to visit you? Sometimes, the brahmin says. Do you offer them food, something to eat? Sometimes, yes. And if they don't accept it, whose is it then? Second, the brahmin's own answer. If they don't accept it, he says, it stays mine. Third, the turn. The Buddha says, in paraphrase: in the same way, you've abused us, who don't abuse, scolded us, who don't scold, and we don't accept it. It's yours, brahmin. It's all yours. Then he adds a picture: someone who answers abuse with abuse is like a host and guest sitting down to share a meal. He won't share that meal. Fourth, what declining means. This isn't ignoring the man. The Buddha heard every word, and he answered. He just refused the role of the one who eats what's served. That leaves the insult exactly where it started. It also leaves the door open, and the sutta shows it: by the end the brahmin asks to go forth himself, and becomes a monk. Put this beside Angulimala. Yesterday, a man stopped harming. Today, a man stops being harmed, at least in the one way that's up to him: by not swallowing the insult and not throwing it back. Forgiveness, here, starts as a polite refusal.
screen: `WHO OWNS A GIFT NOBODY TAKES?` · `IT STAYS MINE.` · `IT'S YOURS, BRAHMIN.` · `NOT EATING WHAT'S SERVED.` · then, large: `YOURS TO KEEP.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one insult that has stuck. A comment about your work, your looks, your choices. Hear it once. Now picture it as a plate of food set in front of you. You don't have to eat it, and you don't have to throw it back across the table. Just leave it on the plate, and let it be carried back to where it came from. Notice your hands, empty. If you pray, you can use your own tradition's words for letting it go. The bell holds the time.
Bharadvaja. The brahmin clan of the man who cursed the Buddha, and whose abuse the Buddha declined to accept. Today's word.
Your line: yours to keep. When a jab comes your way today, leave it on the plate. Don't swallow it, don't throw it back. Yours to keep. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

965.title: The forgiveness chant
965.hook: a Theravada practice: if I've harmed anyone, I ask forgiveness; if anyone harmed me, I forgive (traditional)
965.howItsDone: In Theravada communities, monks and lay people ask one another's forgiveness in set words at certain times, and meditation teachers teach a forgiveness practice that asks, gives and turns forgiveness toward oneself, repeated slowly over time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bharadvaja's unaccepted gift: an insult the Buddha declined, left with the man who brought it. Your line was yours to keep. Did one stay on the plate? Today, a practice that asks and gives forgiveness in the same breath. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

A few short sentences, said slowly, pointing in different directions. If I have harmed anyone, in thought, word or deed, knowingly or unknowingly, I ask their forgiveness. If anyone has harmed me, knowingly or unknowingly, I forgive them. And in some versions, a further line, turned back toward the speaker: for the ways I have harmed myself, I forgive myself. Versions of it are taught in meditation halls today, with roots in Theravada Buddhist practice. Today: the forgiveness chant.
screen: `IF I HAVE HARMED ANYONE.` → `IF ANYONE HAS HARMED ME.` → `AND, IN SOME VERSIONS, MYSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the directions. Out, in, and back. Asking forgiveness, giving it, and turning it toward yourself. The practice doesn't choose between them. It does them together, each time. That matters, because it's easier to do one than the others. Some people find asking easy and forgiving hard. For others it's the reverse. Saying them side by side keeps either from hiding. Second, knowingly or unknowingly. That small phrase does a lot of work. It admits that some of the harm we've done we'll never know about, and that some of the harm done to us was never meant. It forgives without waiting for a full account of who did what. Third, the older roots. In the Pali texts, owning a wrong and having it accepted is part of the path. In the Digha Nikaya, the Buddha tells a king who has confessed a terrible wrong that seeing a fault as a fault, making amends, and holding back in future is growth in the discipline of the noble ones. Monks in the Theravada tradition still ask one another's forgiveness, in set words, at certain times. Fourth, slowly. The practice isn't meant to be said once and checked off. Some teachers, the meditation teacher Jack Kornfield among them, teach repeating it many times, over time, and noticing what resists. A face that won't come into focus. A line that sticks in the throat. That's not failure. It's the part of the work that's still to do.
screen: `ASK, FORGIVE, AND TURN IT BACK.` · `KNOWINGLY OR UNKNOWINGLY.` · `ROOTS IN THE PALI TEXTS.` · `SAID SLOWLY, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · then, large: `I ASK, I FORGIVE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow right down. If you'd like, say these lines slowly, silently or under your breath, leaving a few breaths between them. If I have harmed anyone, knowingly or unknowingly, I ask their forgiveness. Let whatever faces come, come. If anyone has harmed me, knowingly or unknowingly, I forgive them, as far as I'm able today. If it feels right, a last line, toward yourself. Don't force any of it. Just notice where the words flow and where they catch. The bell holds the time.
Theravada. The Buddhist tradition whose monks still ask one another's forgiveness, and whose practice gives this chant its roots. Today's word.
Your line: I ask, I forgive. Say the lines once more tonight before sleep, slowly, and let the faces that come up come up. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

966.title: Confucius' one word
966.hook: Confucius' one word for life: what you don't want done to you, don't do to others (Analects 15.23)
966.howItsDone: Students of Confucius learn the Analects' answer to Zigong as a rule of life, and shu, reciprocity or consideration, is taught alongside zhong, loyalty, as a core of the Master's way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Theravada's forgiveness chant, said slowly in more than one direction. Your line was I ask, I forgive. Who came up when you said it? Today, the end of the week, and a student who asks his teacher for a single word. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

A student wants it short. Zigong, one of Confucius' disciples, written Tsze-kung in James Legge's old translation, asks his teacher whether there is one word that could serve as a rule of practice for all of a person's life. One word. Not a book, not a list of duties. Something you could carry in your pocket. Confucius doesn't tell him the question is too simple. He gives him the word, and then says what it means. Today: Confucius' one word.
screen: `ONE WORD FOR A WHOLE LIFE?` → `ZIGONG ASKS.` → `CONFUCIUS ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Confucius answers: shu. Legge translates it reciprocity. Others render it consideration, or putting yourself in another's place. Second, the rule. Then he spells it out, in Legge's words: "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Notice it's phrased as a don't. It doesn't tell you to press on others whatever you happen to like. It starts from what hurts, and asks you not to hand that on. Third, the pair. Elsewhere in the Analects, in book four, the disciple Zengzi sums up the Master's whole way in two words, loyalty and shu, and says there's nothing more to it. The word Zigong was given is half of that summary. Fourth, why it's here, in a stretch about forgiveness. Shu asks for one move: stand where the other person stood. That's the same move forgiveness keeps asking for. Before judging what someone did, you ask what you'd want if you had done it, and what you'd not want done to you. Look back at this week. A verse said idfa': push back harm with better. The Gita listed kshama among the divine qualities. Kabir named it khima: where forgiveness is, there is God himself. Angulimala stopped. The Buddha left an insult with its owner. A chant asked and gave forgiveness together. And now a single word from China, for standing in someone else's shoes.
screen: `ONE WORD: SHU.` · `WHAT YOU DO NOT WANT DONE TO YOURSELF.` · `LOYALTY AND SHU.` · `STANDING WHERE THEY STOOD.` · then, large: `SHU.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone whose actions you've been judging lately. Picture what they did. Now step, in your mind, into where they were standing: their tiredness, their pressure, what they could see and couldn't. Ask quietly: if I had done this, what would I want from the people around me? And what would I not want done to me? You don't have to change your judgment. Just let it stand next to that question for a while. The bell holds the time.
Shu. Reciprocity, consideration: Confucius' one word, spelled out as what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others. Today's word.
Your line: stand where they stood. Once today, before you react to what someone did, give it one breath first, then answer. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

myth: Confucius' rule says: do to others what you'd like done to you
it's phrased as a don't: what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
Legge translates shu as reciprocity
others render it consideration, or putting yourself in another's place.
Zengzi sums up the Master's way as loyalty and shu
and says there's nothing more to it.

fork.setup: you're Zigong. you ask Confucius for one word to live by for all of life. what does he answer?
options: he says the question is too simple.
shu: what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
he gives you a long list of duties.
fork.reveal: he gives one word, shu, and spells it out as a don't.

original.note: Chinese: shu, reciprocity or consideration, Confucius' one word in Analects 15.23.

trapdoor: what you thought: the golden rule, in Chinese.
what it means: one word, shu, spelled out as a don't: what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
what a scholar hears: shu paired with zhong, loyalty, in Analects 4.15, where Zengzi sums up the Master's whole way.
